# Rapid Agent Development

This document walks you through the rapid agent development process using Google Antigravity \- vibe coding and testing, deploying to Agent Engine and to register the agents with Gemini Enterprise. The process automates the agentic code generation process as much as possible, although not completely hands-off. The developers should understand the technology (specifically ADK) and should be able to verify the generated code before starting to use this approach.

## Technologies

1. **ADK**: A framework to build and test custom agents  
   1. For all ADK resources see [here](https://google.github.io/adk-docs/). This contains quickstarts, example agents and detailed guides on all the ADK capabilities e.g. Sessions and memory, Tools, Context.  
2. **Agent Engine**: Runtime for agents. Documentation [here](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/docs/agent-engine/overview)  
3. **Gemini Enterprise**: Enterprise agentic platform from where end users access agents  
4. **Gemini**: LLM to use to conceptualize, design, and write code  
   1. Recommend to use gemini-3.0-flash (best price, latency and performance tradeoff) by default and gemini-3.0-pro for the root agent/orchestrator. Use pro if you need additional quality from the Flash model.

Prerequisites

1. Install Google Antigravity following the [instructions here](https://antigravity.google/docs/get-started). Also familiarize yourself with how to use Antigravity.  
2. Clone this [github repository](https://github.com/VeerMuchandi/rad-skills) inside `~/.gemini/antigravity`  folder on our workstation. This will download all the skills required for the rapid agent development from the repo. Rename the folder from `rad-skills` to `skills`

   `cd ~/.gemini/antigravity`

   `git clone https://github.com/VeerMuchandi/rad-skills`  
   `mv rad-skills skills`

3. Install google-adk by running `pip install google-adk`

## Define problem

Create your own problem definition. You can use your own words to write the requirements to take help from Gemini.

A couple of examples here:  
(Multi-agent)  
[Automated Grants and Funding Manager](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Uu8AXTMQDODMae0ZxARXN3NgT4_MOtaThUADOCsPXa0/edit?usp=sharing&resourcekey=0-6ckBETPz9V_nGmppauDeRA)  
[DMV Complex Case Triage and Staff Routing](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1YVlpGZU1-VrjFR1fQqj2FxhoDEvpUccit8G_oDsN7Dw/edit?usp=drive_link&resourcekey=0-DbUD5NMCu6rimu4g9IqgYw)  
(Single agent)  
[Phone Plan Shopper](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1OFjxrFNrhtrT_H49P_Q8zt68hGagOoQlMZmvgowPi5Y/edit?usp=drive_link)  
[CareConnect Navigator](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1_GmZ0gkxVEnvse-eWk9slt5EgWWuO3tH8sV_5ZkvW_4/edit?usp=sharing&resourcekey=0-E5yWZ640Xae_ZzMW4J4slQ)

## Create Workspace in Antigravity

Open Antigravity application and use the `Open Folder` option. Choose a pre-created folder or create a new folder at your desired location and open it. Let us name the folder `rad-workshop`. We will use that folder as your workspace.

![][image1] ![][image2]

You can choose to trust the authors of the folder  
![][image3]

And you are now ready to code using Antigravity in this new workspace named `rad-workshop`. We will create our agents in this workspace. We will use the agent manager that is towards the right side of the screen to do agent based development.  
![][image4]

You can choose the Gemini Pro model from the list here.   
![][image5]

## Define architecture

Let us use **Agent Manager** to generate architecture from the use case and review that architecture.

1. In the text box type in the following command to load the skill 

`Load the Agent Architect skills`

	Once the Agent Manager analyzes and loads skills you should see a response that it has loaded. While response would be non deterministic, it would be a message similar to the below:

![][image6]

**Note**: Antigravity requires user approval at different stages. So watch out what it is doing and provide approvals as needed. You can also interrupt by pressing `![][image7]` and suggest course correction, if you think the direction that it is taking is not correct.  
   
Type-in the following prompt:

`For the conceptual requirements given below generate the architecture:`  
 (SHIFT+ENTER for new line)  
*Paste the use case text here (like one of the above examples)*

The Agent Architect in Antigravity interactively analyzes your requirements and asks clarifying questions as necessary.  You will see a plan with a task list like below and it executes these tasks one after the other. You can add review comments to the plan if you want to suggest any changes.   
![][image8]

It will suggest a single agent vs multiple agents architecture with its own reasons and lets you choose the architecture you want. Here is an example for the phone plan shopper concept.

![][image9]

As it generates architecture and creates files, it will ask for permission to save files. You will notice that the architecture is saved into an `agent_architecture.md` file in a folder created for the agent. 

## Review Architecture

You can review that in preview mode if you wish to as it would have figures. You may want to install a mermaid extension to view these figures. Antigravity generates the design and also agent evals that contain scenarios that include success criteria for this agent. 

![][image10]

You can also select portions of the document and chat based on that  
![][image11]

![][image12]

Carefully review the architecture output from the above step and if required prompt the CLI to refine the architecture before moving to the code generation step. 

* In case of multi-agent architectures you want to make sure that the agent introduces itself and collects the required inputs from the user before handing over the control to workflow agents (sequential, parallel or loop agents).  
* You may also want this agent to handle finalization steps like consolidating the work, explaining to the user and asking the user for the next steps.

## Generate code

Let us now continue to use **ADK** **Agent Developer skill** for code generation, refactoring and testing.  Let us explicitly load the skill to make sure by typing in:

`Load the adk agent developer skill` 

In a few seconds, once loaded,  you will see a message like this  
![][image13]

As you can see the skill is designed to check for updates so that it can refresh itself based on the ADK references.

You will also notice that the task list will be updated with the implementation steps. You can always add comments to suggest edits to the implementation plan.  
![][image14]

If you continue conversation with the agent to update the references as needed. It will ask for permissions to run the update script. 

It will also collect additional details (such as **`GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT`** and **`GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION`** environment variables) needed for your agent code generation and testing. Note that the skill is designed to use VertexAI i.e **`GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI="True"`**.  
![][image15]

Once you answer the questions, it will proceed with the agent scaffolding and code generation. This code generation step runs for several minutes depending on your use case. It does the code generation and testing. The code gets added to a new folder that is named based on your use case. Antigravity needs approvals (to proceed with some activity such as creating files/folders or running commands). So, keep watching. It may also ask to create a python virtual environment as it is testing.

![][image16]

**Caution**: Sometimes the generated code may not be completely perfect. So you need to review the code for completeness and iterate through the steps with additional instructions as needed.

If Antigravity hands over the code before completing the testing, you can always prompt it to test by prompting like this:

`Test this agent using 'adk run' from the root folder. Fix any issues and update the architecture as you make code changes. Note that you need to provide a user prompt when you test using adk run. Refer specs`.

**Note**: Antigravity tries to create testrunner code to test. But you can always let it complete and force it to test again using adk run. If your use case involves files to upload, it may be hard to use adk run to test and you may have to switch to adk web based testing.

You can also ask Antigravity to run browser based testing using adk web, by prompting with

`Can you test with adk web in the browser?`

As the code changes can happen multiple times during iterative testing, you want to ensure that the architecture is kept up to date with the changes. While we already instructed to do so, you can always verify by prompting

`Verify and ensure that the architecture saved in agent_architecture.md is up to date with all the changes you made.`   

Just like before you need to watch what Antigravity is doing and you may have to carefully review and `Accept` certain commands  
![][image17]

## Test Locally (manual testing)

Since most of these agents would have mock data to test initially, we can ask Gemini to output the test scenarios to use that are based on this mock data.

`What kind of questions can I ask to test this with adk web? Create a testing.md document in the agent folder with these scenarios.`

Open another terminal and at the root folder level where the agent code got created run the following command to test your agent(s)

`adk web`

This should bring up ADK on your local machine at [http://127.0.0.1:8000](http://127.0.0.1:8000) to test your code locally. 

Alternatively you can also ask Antigravity to run it for you

`Run adk web for me to test`

## Refactor Code (if required)

If you are unhappy with the functionality of the agent, you can either fix it yourself or again use Antigravity’s help to refactor. Note how the task list gets updated as you make functional changes that require refactoring code

![][image18]

## Deploy agent to Agent Engine

Once the agent is built and tested locally using ADK web, the next step is to deploy the agent to Agent Engine, a fully managed runtime on Google Cloud for agents.

Let us ask Gemini to create a `.ae_ignore` file first. 

`Create a .ae_ignore file with all temporary data that should not be used for deployment to the agent engine.`

Once done, verify the contents of the file to make sure it covers all the files that should be ignored during deployment.

`Create a requirements.txt file that includes all dependencies for your agent.`

At this point you have two options for deploying this code:

1. Deploy using **terraform** (suggested)  
2. Deploy using `adk deploy` method which is typically used for development environments.

Pick one of these two approaches.

### Deploy using Terraform

### The skill to deploy using Terraform was installed along with the other skills earlier. Although not required, let us ask Antigravity to explicitly load it first just to make sure it is there. 

### `Load the skill for Agent Engine Terraform deployment`

### Just type in a simple prompt like

### `Let us now deploy this code using terraform to agent engine`

### Note how task list will now get deployment tasks 

### ![][image19]

### It will ask you for permissions to run `terraform init` , `terraform plan` and `terraform apply` commands. It also creates the entire deployment code in the `deploy` folder so that the agent code is separated out from the deployment.

### Alternate option: Deploy using adk deploy

1. Define all the environment variables that your code expects in a `.env` file. Add the following two additional environment variables setting their values to `true`  
*  `GOOGLE_CLOUD_AGENT_ENGINE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY` enables the agent traces and logs, but doesn't include prompts and response data.  
*  `OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT` enables the logging of input prompts and output responses.  
2.  Within the project where you are planning to deploy, create a GCS bucket that will be used for staging your code.

To deploy using \`adk deploy\`manually, open a terminal, make sure you are in the parent folder (`rad-workshop`) from your agent code and run the following command to deploy the agent to Agent Engine:

```
adk deploy agent_engine --project=YOUR_PROJECT_ID --region=us-central1 --staging_bucket=gs://DEPLOYMENT_BUCKET --display_name="YOUR_AGENT_NAME" YOUR_AGENT_FOLDER_NAME
```

You can also prompt Antigravity to deploy using this method by running. This adk deploy approach is built into ADK developer skill.

`Let us deploy this agent using “adk deploy” method into project <<YOUR_PROJECT_ID>>`

The deployment process takes \>10 minutes to complete. You will see that it copies the files from your local directory, builds a container, and deploys the agent to Agent Engine. The deployment process also gives you a link to track the deployment progress using log explorer. If the agent deployment fails, the logs would provide enough information to understand why it failed.

Note the `reasoning-engine` ID that is displayed once the deployment is complete. This is what is used when we want to register the agent with Agentspace. Once deployed, you can also view and manage the agent in the [Agent Engine UI on Cloud Console](https://console.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/agents/agent-engines).

**Note**:

* If you want to redeploy an agent after a code change, you can provide an additional parameter `--agent_engine_id=AGENT_ENGINE_ID`. You can get the `AGENT_ENGINE_ID` (also known as `REASONING_ENGINE_ID`) from the previous run.  
* There is a feature request to stream the deployment logs while the above command is executing.

## Testing the deployed agent

Once the agent is deployed, navigate to the [Agent Engine UI on Cloud Console](https://console.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/agents/agent-engines).

* Select the agent that you just deployed by clicking on its name  
* Enable any APIs  if it shows that it needs to be enabled.  
* Navigate through different sections on the dashboard to understand the features it offers that include agent usage, model usage statistics, tool calls, CPU and memory usage and agent logs  
* Navigate to Playground tab

You can test the agent from the playground tab by typing in a message. You can also create new sessions.

![][image20]

## Agent Logs

As you use the agent, the logs are captured by the Log Explorer. If you navigate to the Dashboard and select “Logs” in the left menu you can see the logs output by the agent.

You can filter logs by severity or search based on specific fields and values. You can also navigate to the Logs Explorer from here if you want, which will filter the logs based on the reasoning engine id.

![][image21]

You can also select a specific log item and choose “Explain this log entry” . This will open up Gemini Cloud Assist that provides you interactive help to further investigate the issue.

![][image22]

![][image23]

To understand different approaches to do logging from an agent and how to analyze agent logs in detail refer [this documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/agent-builder/agent-engine/manage/logging#python-logging_1)

## Agent Engine Traces

As you start using the agent in a session, navigate to the Traces tab to  notice how the traces to different calls are captured and the amount of time spent on each call

![][image24]

You can also traverse through different events and their corresponding traces in the Event tab

![][image25]

\* Navigate to the Traces tab for the agent and you can inspect the trace details, including a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of its spans, inputs and outputs, and metadata attributes.

![][image26]

![][image27]

For more details on Agent Tracing refer to [this documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/agent-builder/agent-engine/manage/tracing).

## Agent Evaluation

Navigate to the Evaluation tab to configure evaluations for the deployed agent. Currently evaluations are created in a Colab notebook using GenAI Eval SDK. You will define datasets specific to your agent with `agent_prompts` specific to your agent. As you run the evaluation, the results from the agent are evaluated and shown along with the metrics.

## ![][image28]

When you click on New Evaluation, you will see a sample Colab that will be set up in the Colab enterprise if you choose to proceed. 

![][image29]

You will have to edit the code in the Colab to make it agent specific and run the Colab. 

![][image30] 

For more information on the GenAI Evaluation Service refer to the [documentation here](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/docs/models/evaluation-overview).

## Registering the Agent with Gemini Enterprise

We offer a Gemini Agent Registrar skill that will handle agent registration with the Gemini Enterprise app. Once the agent is deployed to Agent Engine, simply prompt like as under:

`Register the agent with the Gemini Enterprise App with app id <<GE App Id>>`

You can find Gemini Enterprise App Id from the google cloud console, where you created the app [https://console.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise/apps?project=](https://console.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise/apps?project=your-project-id)YOUR\_PROJECT\_ID

This will register the agent with the Gemini Enterprise app. You can go to the Agents section and find the registered agent. 

**Note**: You still need to click on the agent name and provide access to users so that the agent is visible in the agent gallery as described in the steps 8 through 11 below.

In case you want to manually register the agent with Gemini Enterprise, follow the steps below.

### Manual registration

Gemini Enterprise (GE) provides the Agent Gallery through which the agents can be accessed by the employees of an organization. It provides a centralized space from where the agents are made available to the employees. In order to register the agent with GE, the GE administrator would have to register the agent with Agent Registry in GE. You need a Gemini Enterprise application instance that the employees have access to and where the agent will be registered.

1. Navigate to the Gemini [Enterprise Apps](https://console.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise/apps) section in the Cloud Console. It displays a list of GE apps from which you can choose the specific application where you want to register the agent created above.  
2. Once you select the app, navigate to the `Agents` section within the app  
   ![][image31]  
     
3. It displays the list of all the agents. Now click on `+ Add agent` to register the agent![][image32]  
     
4. You will see different types of agents to add. Choose the `Custom Agent via Agent Engine`.  This allows us to select the agent deployed to the agent engine in the previous step.  
   ![][image33]  
     
5. In case of agents that require authorization (for example an agent that accesses the backend database using credentials), we can create authorization in the next step.  If your agent doesn't need authorization credentials, you can proceed by clicking on `Next`.  
   ![][image34]  
6. Now we can configure the agent by providing the Agent display name, a short description that allows LLM to choose the agent for specific needs, and the reasoning engine id (the full resource name in the format: projects/{project}/locations/{location}/reasoningEngines/{reasoningEngine} ), that was noted in the previous step after deployment. If you missed to copy this you can find it under the `Resource name` for your agent in the  [Agent Engine UI on Cloud Console](https://console.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/agents/agent-engines).

   

   ![][image35]

7. Once you press on `Create` the agent gets registered and it will appear in the list of agents registered with the GE application.  
8. You can now select the registered agent by clicking on the name of the agent.  
9. You can edit the details if you wish to. You can navigate to `User Permissions` tab to provide GE users access to the agent.  
   ![][image36]  
10. You can click on `+ Add user` to choose either specific users, a group of users,  or provide access to all GE users and assign them `Agent User` role. .  
11. Once the access is assigned, the end user can access Gemini Enterprise and the agent will show up in the GE Agent gallery under the  from your organization section.

## Building A2UI agents with RAD

You may have noticed that simple ADK agents offer very textual user interactions. In order to make the agents more attractive and user friendly, we can add rich user interfaces to these  agentic interactions using A2UI. Refer [a2ui.org](http://a2ui.org)

RAD offers skills for A2UI agent development. Currently we have:

* **A2UI UX Designer** : Generates UX design for an ADK agent by analyzing its flow  
* **A2UI Developer** : Generates A2UI Agent code following the UX Design  
* **A2UI Local Tester**: Generates test code including frontend client to test the A2UI agent locally before deployment  
* **Agent Engine Python Deployer**: Currently A2UI agents need custom code to deploy to Agent Engine. This deployer generates the code and all dependencies and handles deployment.  
* **Gemini Enterprise Agent Registrar**: Handles registration of A2UI agent with Gemini Enterprise App  
* **Browser Tester**: Tests the agent in the browser

Following the approach you learnt so far, you can apply the same pattern of invoking the skills in plain natural language to build A2UI agents. Here are step by step some example invocations to build an A2UI agent from a plain ADK agent.

1. Generate UX design invoking the A2UI UX Designer skill. This creates a new folder for the A2UI agent and adds a ux\_design.md including wireframes. You can review the design and interact with the skill further to refine the design until you are satisfied.

   `For the <<agent name>> generate UX design so that we can build A2UI agent for it`

2. Once you are happy with the UX Design, you can build the A2UI agent. The A2UI developer skill will be automatically invoked when you type a prompt  like below. It generates the code in the same folder created for A2UI agent. As the code is generated it is recommended that you review the generated code and understand it. Of special interest is agent\_executor.py that bridges A2A requirements for the agent.  
     
   `Implement this A2UI agent`

3. Next you can run local testing by submitting a prompt like below. This invokes the A2UI local tester skill which creates some code in a subfolder. The code runs the agent and also includes a client renderer that you can use to visualize the rich output. The flow also invokes the browser tester skill to test the agent in the browser. This will allow you to test the workflow of the agent and confirm that the A2UI components in the workflow meet your requirements. Expect multiple turnarounds between this step and refactoring code for your needs as you test

	  
	`Test the agent locally`

4. Once you are happy with the agent functionality, we can deploy the A2UI agent to Agent Engine by prompting as shown below. This will invoke the Agent Engine Python Deployer that generates deployment code and executes it to deploy the agent. Currently the terraform deployer cannot handle the A2UI agent deployments and hence this special skill is used. Note that deployment runs for 10 \- 20 mins. You can check that agent is deployed by navigating to the cloud console under the agent deployments section in your project. If the deployment fails, you can check the deployment logs for the agent.  
     
   `Deploy the agent to project with project id <<your project id>>`  
     
5. Our next step is to register the agent with a Gemini Enterprise app. Run a prompt providing the app id as shown below. This invokes agent registrar skill.  
   

	`Register this agent with Gemini Enterprise App with id <<your GE app id>>`

6. While registering A2UI agents we need to create an OAuth Client (client id and client secret) and assign specific scopes. The skill would not create the OAuth Client by itself, but will give you detailed instructions on how to do it through the cloud console (if it doesn't, you can prompt/ask for specific instructions). Once you provide the client id and client secret it goes ahead and registers the agent with the Gemini Enterprise app.

	`Client id is <<id>> and client secret is <<secret>>`

7. Once the registration is complete, you will have to go to the Gemini Enterprise app, find the agent and assign user permissions manually. Then the agent would be ready to test. When the agent is invoked for the first time after registration, it would require Authorization by the user. So, I suggest you run it yourself on the GE app for the first time.  
     
8. In order to test the agent you can use the browser tester skill by typing in a prompt like below. The browser tester will generate a test plan,  navigate to the Gemini Enterprise URL provided, find the agent and test it. You can always prompt it for additional testing with specific prompting if the test plan it generates is not thorough. Note that the testing is generally slow, but it is good to submit a run in the background as you are doing other tasks.

	`Test the agent end to end in the browser using the Gemini Enterprise app link <<URL>>`

## Additional Material

[Agent Starter Pack](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/agent-starter-pack): This is an open source repository that provides an example of implementing the CICD for Agents, and an approach for Infrastructure setup Evaluation, Deployment and Monitoring, Feel free to adopt it and customize it to your own needs.

## Supplementary GTM Material

### Generate business value pitch

This section addresses how to generate business value pitch from the agent requirements and architecture documents that were produced earlier.

Our objective is to analyze the AI Agent requirements that were used in step 1 and generate a concise, impactful business value pitch for an enterprise buyer (e.g., C-suite, VP, Director). The pitch must be framed in the language of business outcomes, quantifying value wherever possible and focusing on operational and financial impact.

`Load the business value consultant skill`

Once the skill is loaded, let us submit this simple prompt

`Create the business value pitch for <<<>>> agent`

This should generate the business value pitch and save into an md file. Carefully review the output documents generated and iterate as necessary.

### Generate a blog post

In this final step we will generate a blog post for the agent. 

`Load the blog post creator skill`

Once the skill is loaded, type in the following prompt to generate and save a blog post.

`Create a blog post for <<<>>> agent`

This will generate a draft blog post and save it as an md file. 

Thoroughly review the resultant blog post draft and iterate if necessary.
